idiom_name: plain class or dataclass(eq=False); default object identity (is, id())
implementation_notes: Python's object model already implements the in-memory half of the pattern: object.__eq__ is defined as x is y and hash() falls back to id(), so a plain class compares by identity with no code at all. What remains is the identity field: give the entity an immutable id (a UUID or a typed identity value object) assigned in the constructor, or map it with SQLAlchemy, whose Session maintains an identity map guaranteeing exactly one Python object per database identity per session. When detached copies must compare equal, implement __eq__ on the id and define __hash__ consistently; use @dataclass only with eq=False, because a default dataclass generates attribute equality and sets __hash__ to None for mutable classes.
pitfalls: A default @dataclass generates attribute equality over all fields (and sets __hash__ = None for mutable classes), so two snapshots of the same entity compare unequal after any change; use @dataclass(eq=False) or a plain class for entities.
Overriding __eq__ without defining __hash__ - or leaving it as object.__hash__ - makes equal entities hash differently, breaking sets, dicts and the ORM's own collections.
Outside a SQLAlchemy Session the identity map no longer applies, so two queries create two objects for the same row; keep the session or unit of work scoped around the use case.
